sections.body: Artificial intelligence in research and teaching is the use of software to read, organize, analyze, write, and simulate the work that scholars and instructors do. In practice, systems now search literature, summarize papers, build citation networks, transcribe interviews, suggest qualitative codes, run statistical tests, draft grant sections, check references, design course materials, and control or model laboratory experiments. These tools operate on text, data, images, and instruments, and they often sit inside existing workflows rather than replacing them. A researcher might use a model to screen many abstracts, then read the shortlist by hand. A teacher might use a model to generate practice questions, then revise them for accuracy. The field is less about a single autonomous scientist and more about many narrow assistants that need human checking.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work stands unevenly. Search, citation mapping, transcription, and basic code generation are useful and widely tested, though they still miss context and produce confident errors. Literature synthesis remains hard because models can invent citations, overlook negative results, and flatten disagreements across studies. Quantitative analysis can be reproduced when code and data are shared, but many published pipelines are not, and models may choose inappropriate tests. Qualitative analysis benefits from faster coding, yet interpretation, reflexivity, and theory building stay with the researcher. Peer review and grant evaluation are only partly automated, mostly for triage, conflict checks, and formatting, because judgment, confidentiality, and accountability are not solved. The site's library holds 135 research papers, and its pages link to original papers rather than to the Consensus search tool, which reflects the broader rule that claims should be traceable to sources.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Literature Review and Evidence Synthesis is the natural entry point for finding and weighing prior work, while Citation Mapping and Discovery shows how to trace influence, clusters, and gaps across a field. Quantitative Analysis and Reproducible Work covers statistical code, data pipelines, and replication, and Qualitative Analysis and Mixed Methods covers interviews, coding, and the mixing of text and numbers. Grant Proposals and Funding follows the money side, from finding calls to drafting budgets and impact statements, and Academic Writing and Peer Review deals with drafting, revision, reference checking, and the review process. Course Design and Teaching turns the same tools toward syllabi, assessments, and classroom materials, and Research Data and Repositories handles storage, metadata, sharing, and long term access. Laboratory Automation and Simulation covers instruments, robotic workflows, and computational models of experiments, and Governance, Ethics and Research Integrity sets the rules for authorship, bias, privacy, and misconduct across all the other pages. A reader can move from the first page to the last in any order, but the integrity page is the page that applies to every method described here.
